D2 · DSP L04: LCCDEs, Impulse Response and Convolution

Why this matters in the exam: Sample Test 1 Q4 (“DT LTI Systems”) is worth 7 of the 20 marks. It asks for modes [1], output by recursion [2], from the LCCDE [2] and a closed-form convolution [2], all from this lecture. Q3 (4 marks) also needs you to read properties off an LCCDE. Tutorials 2 and 3 practise every part, and the same machinery comes back later in z-transforms (L07–L08) and digital filters (L09). Each part is a fixed procedure, so marks here should be close to guaranteed.

2. The method

Recognise the question. “Characteristic modes” → A. “Using recursion” → B. “Find the output” with a formula input → C. “Impulse response” → D. “Evaluate the convolution” → E (finite sequences) or F (formulas). “Overall impulse response” of a block diagram → G.

A. Characteristic modes

  1. Copy the coefficients into .
  2. Solve. For complex roots, give and .
  3. Write the modes: ; or for a repeated root; or for a complex pair.
  4. Add one line on stability: all means stable; any means unstable.

B. Recursion

  1. Rewrite as .
  2. Draw a table with columns , , the computation and . Use for , or the given ICs.
  3. Evaluate 4–5 samples, then write with the arrow at .

C. Full solution (homogeneous plus particular)

  1. Find the modes (A), then write .
  2. Pick the trial . Substitute it into the full LCCDE, cancel the common factor (for example ), and solve for .
  3. Find by recursion (B) from the given ICs.
  4. Set at and solve the system for the .
  5. State the answer with (or “”), then check one more sample against the recursion.

D. from an LCCDE

  1. No feedback: read off . Done.
  2. Otherwise: (from A).
  3. Run the recursion with and zero ICs to get .
  4. Solve for the . If , the mode form only holds from onwards. Write and fit the extra samples.
  5. Check from the recursion against your formula. Then classify: causal, stable, FIR or IIR.

E. Finite convolution (tabular, “long multiplication”, T3 Q6a)

  1. The output starts at (the sum of the starting indices). Its length is .
  2. Write on the top row. Below it, write , then shifted one place right, and so on. Add the columns. Do not carry digits.
  3. Check that , then mark .

These are the New Q1 sequences. Press Play and watch each build up from the flipped, shifted , then check the result against the long-multiplication table in the Q1 solution.

F. Closed-form convolution (formulas)

  1. Pick the simpler signal to flip. Write with the step functions kept in.
  2. Turn every step into an inequality on (for example and ). These give the summation limits and the range of where the answer is nonzero.
  3. If a signal is finite (for example ), sketch how much it overlaps the other signal. Each overlap stage gives a separate case for with its own limits.
  4. Factor out anything that does not depend on . Write the rest as and apply the geometric sum.
  5. Simplify and attach or the case ranges. Check and .

G. Interconnections

  1. Work from the inside out. Signals that branch and then add are parallel (add ’s). Blocks in series are a cascade (convolve ’s).
  2. Use as a shift, and simplify differences of steps sample by sample.
  3. Then do causality and stability on the overall .

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Modes from the wrong side. The coefficients () never enter the characteristic equation. A system with no terms has no modes. Don’t write “, modes ” and leave it unexplained.
  • Sign flip in recursion. becomes . One sign error ruins every sample after it.
  • Plugging into the closed form. The closed form is only valid for . Always get and by recursion first. T3 Q4 shows why: .
  • Repeated roots. Writing leaves you one equation short. You need . Also watch the course’s notation: is written as .
  • Forgetting the terms when . For , the mode form fits only from (see New Q3).
  • Dropping step limits. only exists for , so the answer needs . Finite pulses need separate cases for . A closed form with no range stated is incomplete.
  • Geometric sum off by one. has terms, so the numerator is , not . If , the formula becomes . Use instead.
  • “Stable” for . , and are all not absolutely summable, so these systems are unstable.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

LCCDE  sum a_p y(n-p) = sum b_q x(n-q), a0=1, order k
MODES  lambda^k + a1 lambda^(k-1)+...+ak = 0   (y-coeffs ONLY; no y-terms => no modes, FIR)
  distinct: C1 l1^n + C2 l2^n | double: C1 l^n + C2 n l^n (l=1: C1 + C2 n)
  complex r e^{+-j th}: r^n (A cos th n + B sin th n)
PARTICULAR  same form as x: K a^n (K n a^n if a is a root), K, K1 cos+K2 sin; sub into FULL eqn
TOTAL  y = yh + yp; y(0..k-1) BY RECURSION from ICs; solve for C's; attach u(n); check y(k)
RECURSION  y(n) = -a1 y(n-1) - ... + b0 x(n) + b1 x(n-1)...  (flip y signs)
h(n)  x=delta, zero ICs. FIR: h=b_n. IIR: modes + h(0..k-1) by recursion.
      m>=k: extra delta(n-i) terms, i=0..m-k
CONV  y(n)=sum_k h(k)x(n-k); steps -> limits on k AND range of n
  finite: start = nx+nh, length Nx+Nh-1, check sum y = (sum x)(sum h)
  sum_{k1}^{k2} r^k = (r^k1 - r^(k2+1))/(1-r)
  a^n u * b^n u = (a^(n+1)-b^(n+1))/(a-b) u(n);  a^n u * a^n u = (n+1) a^n u(n)
  check y(0)=h0x0, y(1)=h0x1+h1x0
PROPERTIES  causal: h=0 n<0 | stable: sum|h|<inf (all |lambda|<1) | FIR always stable
  |lambda|=1 or u(n),(n+1)u(n),cos u(n) => UNSTABLE | static: h=K delta(n)
INTERCONNECT  cascade h1*h2 (any order); parallel h1+h2; x*delta(n-d)=x(n-d)
